n: Should I rest or move with low back pain?
a: Staying as active as possible leads to faster recovery than resting.

n: Is breakfast the most important meal?

n: Does vitamin C help with colds?
a: Regular intake slightly shortens colds (about 8%) but does not make them less frequent. Started once you are ill, the effect is negligible.

n: Is too much vitamin C dangerous?
a: More than 2 g a day often causes diarrhoea and raises the risk of kidney stones. Care is needed with G6PD deficiency and haemochromatosis.

n: Which tests do I need every year?
a: It depends on age and history: blood pressure, lipids, blood sugar, and cancer screening (breast, cervix, bowel) according to guidelines.

n: Can I take antioxidants during chemotherapy?
a: Only with your oncologist's approval. Some may reduce how well the treatment works.

n: What should I eat to lower cholesterol?
a: Oats, legumes, nuts, plant sterols, olive oil instead of butter. Together they can lower LDL by up to 20–30%.

n: Is coffee good or bad for you?
a: For most people, 2–4 cups are linked with lower mortality in observational studies. Take care in pregnancy, with anxiety, arrhythmias and insomnia.

n: How many hours before bed should I stop coffee?
a: At least 6–8 hours. Caffeine 6 hours before bed reduced sleep by about 1 hour.

n: Are cold showers good for you?
a: One large study showed fewer sick days. Other benefits have little data. Avoid with heart disease.

n: What should I do when a cold starts?
a: Rest, fluids, zinc lozenges in the first 24 hours. Fever for more than 3 days or breathlessness need a doctor.

n: Does collagen work for the skin?

n: How much vitamin D do I need?
a: Most adults are covered by 600–800 IU a day, while correcting a deficiency usually takes 1000–2000 IU. Over 4000 IU only on medical advice. A 25(OH)D test shows what you need.

n: Should I take K2 with D3?
a: The combination is popular, but it has not been shown to be better than D alone. If you take warfarin, K2 changes how it works.

n: Do I need to test my vitamin D?
a: Yes, if you are at risk of deficiency (little sun, obesity, osteoporosis, malabsorption, dark skin). For the general population, guidelines do not recommend mass testing.

n: When is the best time to take vitamin D?
a: With the fattiest meal of the day, because it is fat-soluble and better absorbed. The time of day matters less than consistency.

n: Supplements on an empty stomach or with food?

n: How do I improve my endurance quickly?
a: Combine easy aerobic exercise with 1 interval session a week and increase volume gradually. If you smoke, quitting brings quick improvement.

n: Are energy drinks dangerous for teenagers?
a: Yes. A lot of caffeine and sugar, fast heart rate and insomnia. Not for children or teenagers, and never with alcohol.

n: How much exercise do I need a week?
a: 150–300 minutes of moderate or 75–150 of vigorous aerobic exercise, and 2 days of strength training.

n: How do I start exercising from zero?
a: Start with a 10-minute walk a day and increase every week. Add 2 days of simple strength exercises. With heart disease or symptoms, see a doctor first.
